old: This project studies the design and implementation of a Caro web application together with a set of adversarial-search experiments and teaching materials. The report specifies a 15 × 15 Freestyle game, the board and move-history contracts, and the algorithms used to select and evaluate moves. It explains random and rule-based baselines, contiguous-run heuristics, tactical checks, Chebyshev candidate generation, soft candidate caps, Minimax and Alpha-Beta. It also treats iterative deepening, Zobrist hashing, transposition-table bounds, quiescence and incremental pattern counting in their corresponding reference or legacy implementations. Each algorithm is presented with its inputs, state, decision procedure, invariants, complexity, worked examples and limitations.
new: This project develops a web application for Caro on a 15 × 15 board under Freestyle rules and uses the game to study adversarial search. The application combines a React interface, a PixiJS board and a Rust engine compiled to WebAssembly, with search executed in a Web Worker. The report explains board representation, legal moves, win detection, heuristic evaluation, candidate selection, Minimax and Alpha-Beta pruning. It also examines hashing, transposition tables, quiescence and iterative deepening in separate reference and legacy implementations. The recorded native engine experiment contains 816 search measurements, including 408 paired Minimax and Alpha-Beta comparisons and 820 state-restoration checks. Separate records examine agreement between the JavaScript adapter and the WebAssembly binary, browser Worker responses and selected interface interactions. The reference experiments show that fewer visited nodes can coincide with longer execution time when move ranking adds work. They also identify immediate tactics lost by a hard candidate cap and an incorrect score caused by reusing cached entries after the root player changes. These results connect search algorithms to an interactive application and show why candidate policy, state restoration and cache context must be specified alongside search depth.

old: A position consists of 225 cells, each containing empty, X or O. In an array indexed as B[y][x], row-major conversion to a flat logical index is i = 15y + x; the inverse is x = i mod 15, y = floor(i/15). Hence the center (7,7) has index 112, and (14,14) has index 224. The system divides board representation across three specialized structures according to architectural role: (1) the Rust search engine (Board) stores a contiguous 15 × 15 grid of 225 one-byte repr(u8) cells (Empty = 0, Black = 1, White = 2) paired with move_count; (2) the match wrapper (Game) and frontend (GameState) store match progression and an ordered Move history; and (3) the legacy TypeScript bot (BotBoard) uses a 1D sentinel-padded array with directional bitmask segments. The rationale for this division is to decouple high-frequency recursive search from match-lifecycle management. Its primary benefit is O(1) direct indexing, O(1) in-place apply/undo during depth-first search, zero per-node heap allocation, and compact L1-cache locality; the trade-off is that the raw 225-cell matrix does not record chronological move order, requiring the outer Game/GameState layer to maintain history and full-board unindexed scans to take O(N²) time [13].

Its cell values are Empty = 0, Black = 1 and White = 2; the array occupies 225 bytes, while the complete Board also contains the counter and any alignment padding [10], [17]. The frontend GameState instead stores occupied coordinates in a Map and maintains ordered move history [18]. The legacy BotBoard uses a one-dimensional array padded with boundary sentinels. These representations support different operations: direct Rust cell access, frontend match history, and incremental line analysis in the legacy bot.

The documented Rust search makes a copy at its outer entry, while its in-place search relies on restoration of the working board [6]. Cloning the root board once per search request isolates exploratory tree mutations from the live game state, while in-place apply and undo avoid O(N²) board copying at internal nodes.

Why last-move 4-axis ray scanning is used: because any newly formed winning line in an ongoing game must pass through the stone m just placed, scanning at most K − 1 = 4 steps in both directions (+1 and −1) along the 4 axes D = {(1,0), (0,1), (1,1), (1,−1)} inspects at most 4 × 2 × 4 = 32 neighboring cells. old: Why the six difficulty tiers are divided this way: the configuration table is designed around two mathematical principles. First, it separates qualitative decision regimes: Easy (d = 0, Random across all empty cells) provides a non-tactical baseline for beginners; Normal (d = 1, uncapped local neighborhood) introduces 1-ply immediate win/block priority and static heuristic scoring; and Hard through Master (d = 2 to 5, Chebyshev radius r = 2) engage multi-ply Alpha-Beta look-ahead. Second, across the four Alpha-Beta tiers, search depth increases linearly (d = 2, 3, 4, 5) while the soft candidate cap tightens inversely (c = 15, 12, 10, 8). Because an adversarial tree with branching factor c and depth d scales as O(c^d) in the worst case (and O(c^(d/2)) under ideal Alpha-Beta ordering), keeping c = 15 at d = 5 would expand up to 15^5 = 759,375 nodes per turn. Tightening the soft cap to c = 8 bounds the worst-case tree to 8^5 = 32,768 nodes (and ~2,000–5,000 nodes with Alpha-Beta pruning), keeping Web Worker latency within interactive browser budgets (47, 252, 551, and 1,418 visited nodes in 1.1–3.0 ms on the benchmarked midgame fixture). Benefits and trade-offs: this inverse (d, c) scaling delivers smooth skill progression and responsive UI performance while the soft tactical cap max(c, 1, |T|) and frontend tactical prepass guarantee that zero immediate 1-ply wins or blocks are ever dropped; the trade-off is that deeper tiers (Expert, Master) prune lower-ranked quiet positional candidates (ranked below index 10 or 8) in exchange for deeper 4-to-5-ply tactical calculation.

For illustration, a uniform tree of width 8 and depth 5 has 8^5 = 32,768 leaves and 37,449 total nodes before pruning. This is a fixed-width model, not an upper bound for the implemented soft-cap search. The tier timings and actual counters are reported in Chapter 5; configuration alone does not establish a latency bound or a measured progression in playing strength.
